title: It's a jug
hookLine: if you love a jug, say "I love a jug," and if it breaks you won't be thrown (Enchiridion 3)
carry: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is

cards: A mug that nobody else is allowed to use. Chipped, maybe. A gift, maybe.
Somebody's grandmother's. One morning it slips off the counter, and the small crack on the tile floor can land like bad news. Everyone in the kitchen knows it's a mug.
And still. Epictetus, teaching in a Greek town, picked almost exactly this object to start with: not a great loss, a clay pot from the kitchen. Today: it's a jug.

teach.h: SAY WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS.
teach.b: In section three of the handbook, Epictetus says: with everything that delights you, or is useful, or that you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is. Start with the smallest things.
If you're fond of a jug, say: I'm fond of a jug. Then when it breaks, you won't be thrown. The point isn't to love it less.

teach.h: LOVE IT, AND NAME IT TRULY.
teach.b: You can still drink from the good mug every morning; the practice is to name it truly while you have it. Clay breaks; that's part of what clay is.
Said ahead of time, the breaking is a sad thing that happened, not a betrayal. Then the hard part. The same section doesn't stop at jugs.

teach.h: THE HARD LINE: A HUMAN BEING.
teach.b: When you kiss your child or your wife, Epictetus goes on, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being, and then if one of them dies, you won't be overwhelmed.
Readers argue about this line. Some find it cold, a way of guarding the heart against the people it should be open to.
Others hear it as tender: everyone you love is mortal, and saying so can make each goodbye at the door count.
The text itself doesn't settle it, and you don't have to either. Why start small? Epictetus is a trainer, and nobody lifts the heaviest weight on the first day.
Practice on the jug, the phone screen, the favorite sweater, and learn the move where it costs little.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism name a cherished object plainly to themselves, 'this is a cup, and cups break', practicing on small things first.

o: a potter who sold clay jugs in a Greek market
a poet who wrote sad songs about lost things
the teacher who says: name what you love for what it is

games.q: it's a jug — tap the pairs.
p: you are kissing a human being

s: Epictetus says to stop loving things so they can't hurt you
he says to name them truly while you love them.
section three goes on from jugs to the people we love
and readers argue about whether that line is cold or tender.
the handbook says to begin with the biggest losses
it says begin with the smallest things.

games.q: you're starting Epictetus' practice. where does section three tell you to begin?
o: with the people closest to you.
with a small thing, like a jug.
games.why: he begins with a jug and says to start from the smallest things, practicing where it costs little.

practice: Choose one small thing you're fond of, a cup, a pen, a pair of shoes, a plant, and hold it or rest your eyes on it. Name it plainly, without coldness, the way you'd say it's raining: this is a cup, and cups break.
Then notice what's left: you still like it, maybe a little more.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, whose small practice names what you love for what it is, starting with the smallest things, so its breaking doesn't throw you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 3: an earthenware pot or jug.
